sections.content: MATH2351 covers rigorous calculus and real analysis topics, typically including sequences, series, limits, continuity, differentiation, and integration—often from a proof-based perspective. The course emphasizes mathematical rigor and abstract reasoning, introducing students to formal definitions and theorems. If you want to build a strong foundation for higher-level mathematics or theoretical subjects, this course is indispensable. However, the abstraction and proof-heavy material can feel challenging if you’re used to computational math.
sections.teaching: Teaching quality in MATH2351 usually depends on the assigned lecturer or professor. Most instructors are highly knowledgeable and passionate about pure mathematics. Lectures are well-organized, with clear explanations of difficult concepts, though sometimes the pace can feel brisk given the depth of material. TAs typically hold helpful tutorials and office hours, but you’ll benefit most if you actively engage and ask questions, especially when proofs or concepts seem unclear.
sections.grading: Grading is generally fair but demanding. Assessment often consists of problem sets (with an emphasis on proofs), midterms, and a comprehensive final exam. Problem sets are challenging and test understanding rather than rote calculation. Partial credit is given for logical steps, even if a proof is incomplete. The curve can be competitive, given that many students taking this course are mathematically inclined. Consistent effort is required to keep up with the class average.
sections.workload: The workload is considerably heavier than standard calculus courses. Weekly assignments can be time-consuming, especially for students new to proof writing or abstract reasoning. Reading the textbook and reviewing lecture notes after class is essential. Expect to spend significant time (and sometimes frustration) wrestling with homework problems. However, the intellectual payoff is rewarding, especially if you’re interested in math, theoretical computer science, or physics.

The teaching was very clear by professor Chang, and he follows the order and format of the topics as given in the Chasnov- Introduction to Differential Equations book. The professor is easily understandable, with his accent not being too thick.
